blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the table this book has been withholding

segments.text: Six forms. Every one of them built separately, on its own, in its own lesson.

utterances: who: yo. hablar, which gives:: hablo.
who: tú. hablar, which gives:: hablas.
who: él, ella, usted. hablar, which gives:: habla.
who: nosotros. hablar, which gives:: hablamos.
who: vosotros (Spain). hablar, which gives:: habláis.
who: ellos, ellas, ustedes. hablar, which gives:: hablan.

segments.text: Most Spanish courses open with this table. This one has spent thirty-two chapters refusing to show it, because a table you cannot yet fill is a picture of work still to do, and a table you can fill is a picture of ground you hold.
Read it now and there should be no surprises in it. That is the point.
And it is not one verb. Every regular -ar verb in Spanish — thousands of them — runs on these six endings, so this table is the present tense of a large part of the language.

segments.instruction: all six in order, top to bottom
segments.source: [YOU SAY: all six in order, top to bottom]

segments.text: Until the whole set runs without a gap in it.

segments.prompt: How many forms does the present tense of a regular -ar verb have?

feedback.correct: Six — and you built each one separately.

segments.text: Give all six endings. (-o, -as, -a, -amos, -áis, -an.) How many regular -ar verbs does this fit? (All of them.) And why did the table wait until now? (Because every box in it had to be yours first.)
